statement: Two opposite corner squares are removed from an 8 by 8 chessboard. Can the remaining 62 squares be covered exactly by 31 dominoes, each covering two squares?

choices.text: Yes, and there are many ways
choices.misconception: I checked that 62 is twice 31 and assumed the count was the only obstacle.
I assumed a tight fit meant a unique arrangement rather than none at all.

choices.text: Only if the dominoes may overlap
choices.misconception: I looked for a way to relax the rules instead of testing whether the colours allow it.

choices.text: No, because the two removed squares share a colour
No, because 62 is not divisible by 2
choices.misconception: I claimed a divisibility obstacle that does not exist, since 62 is even.

hints: Colour the board and count what a domino must cover.
Every domino covers one square of each colour, so any covered region needs equal numbers of the two colours. Check the colours of the squares that were removed.
Opposite corners are the same colour, so the board is left with 32 of one colour and 30 of the other.

solutions.reliable: Each domino covers exactly one dark and one light square, so a fully covered region must hold equal numbers of each. Opposite corners share a colour, so removing them leaves 32 of one and 30 of the other, and no covering exists. The transferable idea: a colouring gives a quantity every piece must respect, which proves impossibility without any searching.
solutions.elegant: 31 dominoes cover 31 of each colour, and 30 is not 31.

whyOnTest: Colouring arguments prove impossibility in one line where a search would take the whole paper, and the counting-only answer is the trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
